sections.text: # Democratic Backsliding: Causes and Patterns
## The Big Picture

OLD MODEL OF DEMOCRATIC DEATH:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Coup d'état: tanks in the street, generals seize power  │
  │ Clear, sudden, visible — Chile 1973, Greece 1967        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

NEW MODEL (21st century):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ DEATH BY A THOUSAND CUTS:                               │
  │ Elected leader gradually dismantles democratic          │
  │ guardrails while maintaining electoral legitimacy       │
  │                                                         │
  │ Hungary 2010-present                                    │
  │ Turkey 2013-present                                     │
  │ Venezuela 1999-present                                  │
  │ Poland 2015-23 (reversed)                               │
  │ India 2014-present                                      │
  │ US 2016-21 (survived)                                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SPECTRUM:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Liberal      Illiberal   Competitive    Electoral    Closed  │
  │ Democracy    Democracy   Authoritarianm Autocracy  Autocracy │
  │                          (hybrid)                            │
  │ ←────────────────────────────────────────────────────────→   │
  │ diminishing political rights and civil liberties             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
## Levitsky and Ziblatt: How Democracies Die
Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt (*How Democracies Die*, 2018) is the central text:
### The Guardrail Concept

```
DEMOCRATIC GUARDRAILS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FORMAL RULES:              INFORMAL NORMS:
  (written, enforced)        (unwritten, self-enforced)
  ┌────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────────┐
  │ • Constitution     │     │ • Mutual toleration: │
  │ • Election laws    │     │   treat opponents as │
  │ • Term limits      │     │   legitimate, not  │
  │ • Judicial review  │     │   existential threats│
  │ • Free press       │     │                    │
  │   protections      │     │ • Institutional    │
  │ • Anti-corruption  │     │   forbearance:     │
  │   laws             │     │   don't use legal  │
  │                    │     │   powers maximally │
  │                    │     │   just because you │
  │                    │     │   can (filling every │
  │                    │     │   court vacancy,   │
  │                    │     │   using filibuster │
  │                    │     │   on everything)   │
  └────────────────────┘     └────────────────────┘

KEY INSIGHT: Informal norms matter AS MUCH as
  formal rules. A constitution that nobody respects
  is just paper.
```
### The Authoritarian Playbook
Levitsky-Ziblatt identify a pattern across cases:

STEP 1: WIN ELECTION (legitimacy is essential)
  "The paradox of modern authoritarianism:
   it begins through democratic means"

STEP 2: CAPTURE THE REFEREES
  • Pack courts with loyalists
  • Appoint loyalists to election commissions,
    anti-corruption agencies, central banks
  • Replace professional civil servants with
    political loyalists

STEP 3: SIDELINE OR DESTROY OPPONENTS
  • Use legal system selectively against opponents
    (prosecute rivals on corruption charges — often
    real, but selectively enforced)
  • Defund or pressure civil society organizations
  • Use regulatory agencies against critical businesses

STEP 4: REWRITE THE RULES
  • Change electoral laws to favor incumbents
    (gerrymandering, voter ID, reducing polling places
    in opposition areas)
  • Weaken or eliminate term limits
  • Change constitution to entrench new order

EACH STEP LOOKS LEGAL: "Unlike the crude
  authoritarians of the 20th century, the would-be
  autocrats of today are skilled politicians.
  They don't destroy democracy — they subvert it,
  step by small step."
```
### The Role of Political Parties as Gatekeepers

Historically, political parties filtered out authoritarian candidates before they could capture democratic politics. Both US parties rejected demagogues internally in 1920s-40s (Father Coughlin, Huey Long). The breakdown of party gatekeeping is key to Trump and Orbán's success.
## Mounk and Yascha Mounk: People vs. Democracy
Yascha Mounk (*The People vs. Democracy*, 2018):

**Two things coming apart that used to go together**:
1. **Liberal democracy**: Rights-protecting institutions constraining what majorities can do
2. **Popular sovereignty**: What the majority wants, governs

```
MOUNK'S DIVERGENCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  LIBERAL DEMOCRACY           SPLITS INTO TWO PATHOLOGIES:
  (rights + popular             │
   sovereignty)                 │
                    ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                    ▼                       ▼
        ILLIBERAL               UNDEMOCRATIC
        DEMOCRACY               LIBERALISM
        ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐
        │ Electoral        │    │ Expert techno-  │
        │ majorities       │    │ cracy without   │
        │ override         │    │ democratic      │
        │ individual       │    │ accountability: │
        │ rights:          │    │                 │
        │ Hungary, Poland, │    │ EU institutions,│
        │ India, Turkey    │    │ central banks,  │
        │                  │    │ IMF structural  │
        │                  │    │ adjustment      │
        └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘
  The cure for undemocratic liberalism (give people more
  say) can produce illiberal democracy (majority vote to
  strip rights from minorities).
```
## V-Dem: Measuring Democratic Backsliding
The Varieties of Democracy project (V-Dem, Gothenburg) is the systematic measurement approach.

```
V-DEM FRAMEWORK
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FIVE COMPONENTS OF DEMOCRACY:
  1. Electoral (free and fair elections)
  2. Liberal (individual rights, rule of law, checks)
  3. Participatory (civil society, direct democracy)
  4. Deliberative (reasoned public debate)
  5. Egalitarian (equal protection and access)

AUTOCRATIZATION WAVES (V-Dem measurement):
  Third Wave of Democratization: 1974-2008
  ~35 countries democratized; ~25% increase in democracies

Democratic Recession: 2008-present
  ~42 countries have backslid since 2010
  World share of population living under autocracy: ~70%
  (V-Dem figure; Freedom House figure lower — see note below)

KEY FINDING: Autocratization is more common
  than previously thought, but pace is gradual —
  most cases take 5-10 years to full autocracy
```

**V-Dem vs. Freedom House measurement distinction**: V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy, Gothenburg) and Freedom House use different operationalizations, which produce different regime classifications for borderline cases. V-Dem reclassified India as an "electoral autocracy" starting in 2018, driven by declines in its liberal component indicators (judicial independence, media freedom, minority rights) even while national elections remained competitive. Freedom House rates India "partly free" — a less severe classification — because its electoral component indicators remain stronger. The ~70% of world population living under autocracy figure is V-Dem's and is driven substantially by this India classification. Freedom House's figure for the same period is lower. Neither is wrong; they're measuring different things. V-Dem's liberal democracy index puts heavy weight on institutional constraints on the executive and civil liberties; Freedom House's political rights index weights electoral competitiveness more heavily. Which you use determines both the global aggregate and the classification of large-population borderline cases like India, Turkey, and Hungary.
## Case Studies
### Hungary: Orbán's Blueprint
Orbán's Fidesz won supermajority (2/3) in 2010:

```
HUNGARY AUTOCRATIZATION TIMELINE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  2010: Fidesz wins 2/3 majority → constitutional power
  2011: New constitution passed without opposition input
  2011: Electoral law changed (single-round system, redrew
        constituencies to favor Fidesz)
  2011-13: Constitutional Court stripped of powers;
            packed with Fidesz loyalists
  2013: "Fundamental Law" entrenches Fidesz power
  2014: Media oligarchs aligned with Fidesz acquire
        critical media; state advertising goes only
        to pro-Fidesz outlets
  2016: Soros-funded NGOs targeted (anti-NGO law)
  2017: Central European University forced out of Hungary
  2018: Fidesz retains supermajority — electoral system
        had made this predictable
  2020: Emergency powers during COVID used to rule by decree
  2022: Fourth consecutive supermajority
Orbán explicitly theorized his project: "illiberal democracy" was his own term (2014 Băile Tușnad speech). Referenced Singapore, China, and Turkey as models.
### Turkey: Erdoğan's Consolidation
Erdoğan's AKP won 2002 on moderate Islamist platform. Gradual consolidation:

- 2007-13: "Ergenekon" and "Balyoz" trials prosecuted secular military officers (genuinely accused of coup plotting, but also served to remove checks on AKP power)
- 2013: Gezi Park protests — crackdown; Erdoğan accuses foreign conspiracies
- 2016: Coup attempt (Gülenist?) → mass purges: 150,000 arrested or fired; state of emergency
- 2017: Constitutional referendum → presidential system; removed parliamentary oversight
- 2023: Won presidential election despite economic crisis (inflation >80%)
### Poland: Backsliding Reversed?

Law and Justice (PiS) won 2015 election:
- Packed Constitutional Tribunal (2015-16)
- Judicial reform that gave parliament control over court appointments
- State media became propaganda arm
EU threatened sanctions; Polish courts resisted. Critical difference from Hungary: **Polish civil society stronger**, courts more independent, opposition more organized.

2023: Opposition coalition won parliamentary election; Tusk PM. Attempted to restore judicial independence — but courts packed by PiS complicated reversal. Demonstration that backsliding can be reversed, but reversal is hard.
## Bridges: Democratic Backsliding as Security Failure

**Formal rules + informal norms → defense-in-depth**: Levitsky-Ziblatt's two-layer guardrail model maps directly to layered security architecture. Formal rules (constitution, election laws, judicial review) are the outer perimeter — explicit, documented, enforcement-backed. Informal norms (mutual toleration, institutional forbearance) are the inner layer — the trust and culture that operate when the outer layer is technically being respected but in bad faith. Defense-in-depth works because a determined attacker who breaches the outer perimeter still faces the inner layer; but the inner layer is weaker against an attacker who has legitimate credentials. When an elected leader attacks the informal norms — packing courts *legally*, using regulatory agencies against opponents *within the letter of the law* — they have breached the outer perimeter from the inside. The defenses were designed for external attack (coups), not insider threat.

**The autocratization playbook → privilege escalation attack via legitimate access**: The step-by-step autocratization sequence is a textbook privilege escalation attack: (1) gain legitimate access (win election), (2) use legitimate access to capture the authentication/authorization layer (pack courts, appoint loyalists to election commissions — capture the referees), (3) use the captured authorization layer to exclude adversarial principals (prosecute opponents, defund civil society), (4) rewrite the authorization rules to entrench the access you've acquired (change electoral law, amend constitution). At no step is a rule visibly broken — each step is technically legal. This is precisely the pattern of insider threat modeling: the attacker is operating inside the trust boundary with valid credentials, so signature-based detection (coup-watching) fails. Detection requires anomaly detection on sequences of individually-legitimate actions that in combination escalate privilege beyond any intended limit.

**Democratic resilience factors → insider threat countermeasures**: The institutional factors that make democracies resilient — federal structure (redundant authority nodes), independent judiciary (separate authentication root), independent media (out-of-band communication channel), robust civil society (parallel trust networks) — are exactly the architectural properties that limit insider threat damage. An attacker who has captured the executive cannot unilaterally capture a federal system because state governments are independently provisioned. An attacker who has captured the executive cannot unilaterally capture an independent judiciary because judicial appointments are staggered and terms are long. Poland in 2015-23 is the case where the inner layer (civil society, judiciary resistance) held long enough for an electoral reversal; Hungary 2010-present is the case where the inner layer was breached quickly enough that electoral reversal became structurally improbable.
## Why Some Democracies Survive

INSTITUTIONAL:              POLITICAL:
  ┌────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────┐
  │ • Federal structure │      │ • Opposition parties │
  │   (state govts as   │      │   united, not     │
  │   resistance nodes) │      │   fragmented      │
  │                     │      │                   │
  │ • Independent        │      │ • Norm-upholding │
  │   judiciary with     │      │   faction within │
  │   strong tradition   │      │   incumbent party  │
  │                     │      │                   │
  │ • Free press with   │      │ • Civil society   │
  │   economic           │      │   robust (unions,  │
  │   independence       │      │   churches, NGOs)  │
  │   from state         │      │                  │
  │                     │      │ • Elite defection │
  │ • Civil society      │      │   from autocrat  │
  │   organizations      │      │   (business, mil.) │
  └────────────────────┘      └────────────────────┘

## Decision Cheat Sheet

| If you need to diagnose... | Start With | Key Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Democratic backsliding | Elected leaders dismantling constraints while keeping elections | Bad governance or corruption is not backsliding unless institutions are degraded. |
| Informal democratic norms | Mutual toleration and institutional forbearance | Legal power can be anti-democratic when maximized against constitutional spirit. |
| Backsliding speed | V-Dem gradual 5-10 year autocratization patterns | Gradualism makes real-time recognition and coordination harder. |
| Hungary versus Poland | Constitutional majority, court/civil society strength, EU leverage | Cases diverge because institutions and opposition capacity differ. |
| Populist backlash to technocracy | Mounk's undemocratic liberalism | Technocratic insulation can provoke backlash without justifying autocratization. |
| Democratic resilience | Courts, media, unified opposition, civil society, ruling-party norm keepers | Norm-upholding insiders can matter as much as formal checks. |
